title: After opposing redistricting, state Senate president faces toughest primary yet
summary: Sailboat charter captain and social media personality Bobby LaPin is Senate President Bill Ferguson's biggest challenge since Ferguson was the baby-faced 27-year-old who unseated an entrenched incumbent in 2011, but LaPin still faces extremely long odds.
content:
by Bryan P. Sears and Christine Condon, Maryland Matters June 20, 2026

by Bryan P. Sears and Christine Condon, Maryland Matters June 20, 2026

With less than a week remaining until Election Day, Bobby LaPin’s pitch is simple.

“I’m a Bernie Sanders. He’s a Chuck Schumer,” LaPin says to a pair of voters sipping drinks in Baltimore’s Cross Street Market on a balmy Wednesday afternoon.

“Sold,” one says quickly, chuckling.

LaPin, a Baltimore sailboat charter captain and social media personality, is speaking of Maryland Senate President Bill Ferguson (D-Baltimore City). This year’s primary race against LaPin represents the most difficult challenge Ferguson has faced since he was the baby-faced 27-year-old challenger who unseated an entrenched incumbent in 2011.

LaPin, wearing a military-themed Orioles cap and a “No Kings” T-shirt, along with a pair of flip-flops, worked his way through the market, parking on barstools, plopping down at tables and sidling up to lunch counters. Several passersby recognized him from TikTok or Instagram, where he is the star of self-filmed videos focused on city life.

A self-styled progressive, LaPin is running to Ferguson’s left. He has leveraged his social media following into a grassroots campaign, challenging the veteran politician on issues including affordability, immigration issues and midcycle congressional redistricting.

This year, Ferguson stuck his neck out, opposing redistricting on legal grounds, despite a pressure campaign from Maryland Gov. Wes Moore (D) — and even a visit from U.S. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries.

A redistricting plan, which Democrats hoped would flip the state’s only Republican-held congressional seat, passed handily through the House of Delegates earlier this year, but never reached the Senate floor.

Recently, Ferguson has reversed course, indicating that he is open to calling legislators back to Annapolis for a special session this summer on redistricting, after the U.S. Supreme Court “gutted” the Voting Rights Act.

“He doesn’t see the forest for the trees, and here we are reacting when everyone — anyone — that’s been paying attention, knows that it was a likelihood that voting rights would be stripped by the Supreme Court,” LaPin said in a recent interview.

LaPin faces an uphill battle. Outside money has flooded in to support the incumbent, including a significant sum from a political action committee funded by sports betting companies. Local progressive groups haven’t jumped to LaPin’s aid – even those who were irked that Ferguson jammed up redistricting. In fact, they haven’t even endorsed him.

Moore, who sparred with Ferguson repeatedly on redistricting, did not endorse the senate president. But he didn’t endorse LaPin either.

LaPin’s own polling, conducted in the first week of June, shows him behind Ferguson, 61% to 32%.

LaPin’s camp touts another figure. After likely Democratic voters heard a positive biography, the numbers flipped, showing LaPin on top, 52% to 45%.

Alli Smith, Ferguson’s campaign manager, called LaPin’s messaging about the poll as “dishonest.”

“A lot of noise is this pattern of partial or skewed information that his [Ferguson’s] opponent seems to present to voters,” Smith said. “If you’re asking people to trust you with their vote, facts matter.”

For his part, LaPin said he’s hopeful his campaign has reached enough voters to bring the 52-45 figure closer to reality.

“Since that poll came back, there’s been two mailers, tens of thousands of phone calls, and we probably knocked on 6,000 more doors,” LaPin said.

Similarly, Smith said Ferguson’s ground game targeted a core of group of thousands of voters in the district. Those homes have been visited in recent months by Ferguson or volunteers as many as four times.

Ferguson’s poll of likely Democratic voters in the district conducted by Patinkin Research on June 2 puts Ferguson up 53% to 28% over LaPin.

“Looking at the whole picture of their poll, the data isn’t very far off from what ours was showing,” Smith said.

Ferguson, who has led the Senate since 2020, faces his first primary challenge since 2014. The campaign against Bobby LaPin may be his toughest race since 2010, when it was Ferguson seeking to unseat seven-term Sen. George W. Della Jr.

The rivals engaged in a bitter generational campaign pitting the old guard institution against youthful vision. Ferguson won the 46th District seat by 18 points.

He faced a primary challenge in 2014. He defeated Mateen Rasul Zar, a physician, by almost 80 percentage points.

Ferguson ran unopposed in the next two elections. Smith, who managed the Ferguson campaign in 2014, acknowledged the challenge from LaPin represents a change.

“I would say that this is the most notable challenge since 2010,” she said. “So the first time as an incumbent having to run a campaign, that is about asking for people to vote for you.”

Over the last two elections, Ferguson ran unopposed and focused more on promoting the district “team” with three delegates.

“It was really mainly campaigning on turning out votes for his team members and using a lot of ‘we’ language rather than claiming this explicit credit for a lot of the work that he has done,” Smith said. “He’s very good at sharing credit when he speaks about accomplishments. He has had to learn to talk about his own achievements very explicitly, because it’s his job now that he’s asking people for a vote.”

LaPin, who is also a military veteran, is a twice unsuccessful candidate. In 2014, he ran for the House of Delegates in the 40th District, an area that is more north and west of the district he is now running in. In 2006, he was briefly a candidate for a House seat in Harford County. He withdrew before the primary.

He’s hopeful that after his third race, he will have toppled a political giant. But he’s been frustrated by the lack of support from progressive groups.

“There’s a quote: ‘Never meet your heroes,’” he said.

He fears that key groups were too fearful that Ferguson would prevail, and they would rupture their relationship with the Senate president.

“They’d rather have access than actually stand on their values — and that was crazy to me,” LaPin said.

Larry Stafford Jr., executive director of Progressive Maryland, said the small organization must be “strategic” about the races it chooses to enter. The group’s effort to support Will Jawando for Montgomery County executive, and Wala Blegay for the open congressional seat of retiring Rep. Steny Hoyer (D-5th), have been particularly work intensive, he said.

“We’ve just got a ton of races that we’re focusing on where we’re already facing very tough obstacles,” Stafford said. “We support in races where we believe we can especially move the needle.”

LaPin was especially saddened by the decision from CASA in Action for Maryland, the political arm of the prominent immigrant rights group. LaPin says that it was ICE activity in his close-knit Upper Fells Point community that drove him back to politics. Ferguson’s opposition to redistricting was, as he puts it “icing on the cake.”

LaPin was a vocal advocate for the Community Trust Act, aimed at reining in immigration enforcement. The bill passed this year in a flurry of last-minute activity.

“It was enraging to all the CASA members, all the people that I marched with and stood in protest with … the hundreds of thousands of people that saw my teary-eyed video begging Bill Ferguson to pass the Community Trust Act. It was a complete betrayal,” LaPin said.

Cathryn Jackson, policy director for CASA in Action, said at the time that CASA’s board looked at the “totality” of Ferguson’s tenure in the Senate.

“Since he became Senate president, Maryland has passed legislation that has made a real difference in people’s lives,” Jackson said. “These are all victories that ultimately Bill Ferguson got on board with and delivered.”

Whatever happens, it’s clear that LaPin’s decision to enter the race has forced Ferguson into the most uncomfortable position yet in his 16-year political career.

“We should credit Bobby LaPin for lighting a fire under Bill,” said Robbie Leonard, a Baltimore County attorney and Democratic National Committee member who supports LaPin. “The question will be: If Bobby is not successful, is that fire still there?”

Underlying LaPin’s optimistic polling is an assumption that the upstart candidate has the time and money — he reported raising nearly $188,000 with about $30,000 left on hand — to get that message out before the June 23 primary.

It also assumes that Ferguson, a prolific fundraiser with more than $900,000 in the bank as of Friday, cannot or will not respond.

And the stack of cash Ferguson has in reserve does not include more than $300,000 spent on his behalf by outside groups.

LaPin has slammed Ferguson for accepting donations from corporations such as Baltimore Gas & Electric. He argues that he can lower prices by cutting into corporate profits.

“My best campaign flyer is our BGE bill,” LaPin told a security guard inside the Federal Hill market on Wednesday — handing him a real campaign flyer nevertheless.

For the past two weeks, Ferguson has benefited from mailings supporting his campaign sent to voters in his South Baltimore District. Targeted television ads have also appeared on local cable providers. One of the groups, American Future, a Dallas-based political action committee, paid for the ads backing Ferguson.

PACs such as American Future can spend almost unlimited amounts of money supporting or opposing a candidate or issue. The group can spend the money on mailings, television and online ads — but they cannot coordinate with a candidate’s campaign.

So far, American Future boasts a state campaign fund of $4.75 million, according to the Maryland State Board of Elections, and it has pumped more than $1.6 million into backing Maryland Democrats.

The money is part of $41 million in transfers from the Win for America PAC. Backers of the group include FanDuel, DraftKings and other gaming interests, according to the Federal Election Commission.

Of that, almost $290,000 has been spent in support of Ferguson, who has opposed legalizing internet gaming in the past.

Gaming expansion, which would require an amendment to the Maryland Constitution, could become an issue again in 2027, as the state grapples with billions in projected structural budget gaps over the coming three years.

In addition to support from American Future, the Maryland Realtors Independent Expenditure Committee spent another $55,000 on mailings into his district in support of the Senate leader. More than half the money that funds the Annapolis-based group comes from the National Association of Realtors.
